title: Price Lookup
statement: A store keeps 500,000 product prices and checks thousands of times a second whether a given price exists. Prices are also added during the day, and the store sometimes needs them in increasing order.
examples: List every price from cheapest to most expensive

approaches.name: A balanced binary search tree
approaches.hint: Keep the data ordered as you insert
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: O(log n) per lookup and insert
approaches.why: Lookups and inserts stay logarithmic, and an in-order walk gives the prices in order whenever needed.

approaches.name: A sorted array with binary search
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Fast lookups and ordered output, but each insert shifts many elements.

approaches.name: An unsorted list, scanned for each lookup
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Thousands of full scans of 500,000 prices each second is far too slow, and the order is lost.

title: Deepest Folder
statement: A file browser stores folders as a binary tree (each folder has at most two subfolders). Report how many levels deep the deepest folder is.
examples: A root with two empty subfolders has depth 2

approaches.name: Recursion: 1 + the deeper of the two subtrees
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: Every folder is visited once, and only the current path is kept on the call stack.

approaches.name: Level-order traversal with a queue, counting levels
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Also correct and linear; it holds a whole level in the queue instead of one path.

approaches.name: Count the folders and take log2 of the count
approaches.hint: Use the size of the tree
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: That only matches a perfectly balanced tree; a chain of 10 folders has depth 10, not about 3.

title: Org Chart Floors
statement: An org chart is a binary tree. The company wants to print every manager level on its own line, from the CEO down, left to right.
examples: CEO; then two vice presidents; then their reports

approaches.name: Breadth-first with a queue, one level per round
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: The queue holds exactly one level at the start of each round, so levels come out in order.

approaches.name: Depth-first, passing the depth and appending to that level's list
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Also correct: visiting left before right keeps each level in left-to-right order.

approaches.name: In-order traversal printed as one list
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: In-order mixes the levels together; it does not group people by level.
